name: Juggle (too many channels)
what: Platform logos orbit the frame, each one drops in on the word that names it, then they crowd together with a shake when the speaker reaches the problem.
when: The landscape and first-cut language, on a 'too many channels' line. Do not move this idea to logos circling the speaker's head in a vertical short.
why: It survived every review round of the first short untouched.

name: Logos circling the speaker
what: Logos born behind the speaker's head, then turning around it, half behind and half in front, with a panic speed-up and a fling out of frame.
when: Never. Do not propose circling logos again without asking the user first.
why: Rejected as looking like generic AI filler.

name: Wall of big logos
what: Big logos landing one after another, in front of the speaker or behind them, in place of the orbit.
when: Never.
why: Tried in place of the orbit and refused too.

name: Counters (which channel works)
what: One column per channel with a number spinning up under each; one column can be a dud that turns red, goes grey and is kicked out of frame.
when: Only with the user's real numbers. Real numbers, or no beat.
why: Status not written in the docs. A reference cut lost this beat because its figures were placeholders.

name: Crowd (you would need a team)
what: A grid of plain black silhouettes lands with a running count in a pill, then a red strike crosses the block.
when: On a line about needing a team you do not have. Plain silhouettes, never a mascot repeated.
why: Status not written in the docs.

name: Lockup (naming the product)
what: A mark lands in a yellow disc, the name appears under it, a yellow underline draws itself and a subline types in with a cursor.
when: Once, when the speaker names the product. Use the partner's own logo through a small custom beat (brand-kit.md).
why: Status not written in the docs.

name: Hats (one person, several roles)
what: One portrait in a disc, one variant per role wiped in from the top, each with a pill label.
when: Only with variants of ONE base image (same pose, framing and crop, only the hat or prop changed). It has to earn its place.
why: Status not written in the docs. One reference cut dropped it as one visual too many; independent images read as different people.

name: Map primitives (focus, badges, pulse, boom)
what: Shared helpers for custom figures: push into one brick, a yellow chip under a brick, data flowing back to the hub, the whole map flaring at once.
when: Pulse once, on the line about measurement; boom once per video, on the payoff; a badge is a claim, so make it true.
why: Status not written in the docs.

name: Skills panel and Claude Code terminal
what: A panel slides in beside the map, one skill is picked and it expands into a terminal that runs it.
when: When the video shows a skill being run. Skill names must be real names from this repo; ticks are drawn as vector strokes.
why: Status not written in the docs.
doc: references/beat-catalog.md § Set-piece: the skills panel + Claude Code terminal

name: Headlines at the top
what: Each sentence becomes a screen of 1 to 3 lines at the top of the frame, word by word on the onsets, in Impact capitals, passing behind the speaker's head.
when: Every vertical short in the vertical language, in place of bottom subtitles.
why: The reviewer asked for big text at the top instead of timid subtitles; corrected four times the same day, each correction a verdict.

name: One script accent per screen (Sacramento)
what: One word per screen in the Sacramento script face, written across the line above it, drawn at the same x-height as Snell.
when: One accent per headline screen, on its own line. Across a yellow word, never white on white.
why: The reviewer liked Sacramento, after rejecting Snell Roundhand Black and comparing Lobster.

name: Snell Roundhand Black as the second face
what: Snell Roundhand Black used as the script accent face beside Impact.
when: Never as the secondary face; Sacramento replaced it.
why: Rejected by the reviewer as the secondary face.

name: Script accent beside Impact on one line
what: A script word set on the same line as Impact words, side by side.
when: Never. One face per line: the accent is a line of its own, above or below the Impact line.
why: « of using MY PLATFORM. » side by side was refused: it reads left to right, the rest of the short reads top to bottom.

name: Discreet subtitles on an illustrated plate
what: While a paper plate is up, the headline steps down to discreet Impact subtitles, 66 px, in ink, word by word with no pop.
when: On every illustrated plate: no combination of big headlines and illustration.
why: With an illustrated screen, doing both was too much.

name: Shade at the top of the room
what: An edgeless gradient behind the speaker that puts the ceiling and the window in shadow, so white headlines hold.
when: Under white headlines on a bright room, in the vertical language (in place of the progressive blur).
why: Without it, Impact's white does not hold on these shots.

name: Real capture out from behind the speaker
what: The real screen capture starts inside the speaker's silhouette, slides to its place, then goes back where it came from.
when: When the speaker names their product. Never on a shot where the speaker already shows the screen; with a laptop in hand, run matteHoles first.
why: Part of the vertical language. A capture over a real screen the speaker held up was removed because it made no sense.

name: Stop-motion on the paper
what: What is on a paper sheet moves at a low frame rate (8 poses a second), every pose held and changed on the same frames, like paper cut-outs.
when: Stickers and felt marks on a paper plate. The paper and the subtitles stay smooth.
why: The reviewer wanted the elements to move a little as they enter, but not smoothly.

name: Stop-motion pose sounds
what: Each pose makes a sound: the pack's click on a landing, a fading tick for each settle pose, and one soft felt glide for a whole mark.
when: With stop-motion stickers and marks (stepFps above 0); they are emitted by the figures themselves.
why: Still open: the reviewer's opinion on the paper plate's sounds.

name: A felt sound on every pose
what: A felt-tip sound repeated on each pose of one drawn mark.
when: Never. A mark is ONE soft felt glide from its first pose to its last.
why: It made one arrow sound like a burst of little strokes, a rhythm the video does not have.

name: Camera flash on a change of shot
what: The picture rises to white late and fast (peak 0.82), holds over the cut and comes down, with the pack's camera-flash sound on the cut.
when: On a change of shot, not on every hard cut (on a short full of jump cuts it would be a strobe).
why: The rule from the video that came with the SFX pack, asked for by the reviewer.

name: Old-school hook (CRT TV)
what: The first seconds play through an old TV: curved glass, a halo, a colour fringe, scan lines and a rolling bar, until the flash brings everything back to today.
when: A bonus, asked every time, never on by default; first seconds only, around 7 s, never past 10 s.
why: The reviewer asked for an old-radio effect, then preferred a cathode-ray TV (crt is his pick), then said it is optional.

name: Film and VHS hook looks
what: Two other presets of the old-school hook: washed-out Super 8 at 12 fps with grain and scratches, or a soft 30 fps VHS with a tracking band.
when: Only as an alternative to crt when the user asks; film keeps a little colour (pure sepia turns yellow khaki).
why: Compared beside crt; crt was the reviewer's pick. Not refused in the docs.

name: Old-radio voice on the hook
what: The voice of the hook goes through an old radio set (the am preset: band-passed, driven, a little hiss and crackle), loudness-matched, joined back in a silence under the flash.
when: A bonus with the old-school hook, asked every time, never assumed.
why: The reviewer asked for it; am was his pick among fm, am and walkie.

name: Opening de-zoom, then punches
what: An opening de-zoom from 1.30 to 1.00 in 0.62 s with its whoosh, then a punch (1.12 to 1.14 in about 0.1 s) only on a word that carries the argument, released on the next phrase.
when: Every vertical short in the vertical language; anchor on the speaker's eyes (about 0.27).
why: Part of the vertical language, the reviewer's verdicts.

name: A running list of zoom levels
what: About one zoom move per sentence, amplitude 1.03 to 1.16, linear ramps of 0.12 to 0.50 s, anchored near the top of the head.
when: The landscape intro and the first subtitle cuts only. A vertical short uses the de-zoom and punches instead.
why: Measured on a real cut and held up in review; replaced in vertical shorts by the vertical language (2026-09-29).

name: Progressive blur behind a graphic
what: The top band is blurred and dimmed through a vertical gradient and a time gate, one blur window per beat, so a graphic separates from a bright background.
when: The landscape and first-cut language. Not in a vertical short (blurBand 0, shade() instead).
why: The house answer to separation; a gradient reads as depth instead of a rectangle.
doc: references/motion-language.md § Progressive blur, never a plate

name: A black plate behind a graphic
what: A solid dark rectangle behind an overlay to make it readable.
when: Never. Use the progressive blur, a shade, or a dark underlay stroke for thin lines.
why: It reads as a slide and was rejected every time.
doc: references/motion-language.md § Progressive blur, never a plate

name: A bottom caption line on a vertical short
what: Timid subtitles at the bottom of the frame as the main text of a vertical short.
when: Never in the vertical language: the words are headlines at the top.
why: The reviewer found bottom subtitles too timid.

name: Clean caption style
what: White captions, weight 800, 66 px, a yellow hot word and a 9 px black outline, built from words.json.
when: The subtitle layout of the first cuts (2026-09-03), and any edit that keeps bottom captions.
why: The default; won every review.

name: Karaoke captions
what: A yellow box moving word by word over the caption.
when: Never on a talking head.
why: Rejected as noisy on a talking head.

name: Every cue on a word onset
what: Every graphic lands on the onset of its word from words.json, checked against the audio envelope; never a round number picked by feel.
when: Always. 40 ms early is invisible; 120 ms late reads as lag.
why: Measured on real cuts and held up in review; transcripts misdate word starts by up to half a second.

name: Spring in, ease out
what: Entrances use one overshoot then settle over 0.5 to 0.7 s, exits ease in-out over 0.4 to 0.5 s, sequenced elements 0.16 s apart, all with the shared easing helpers.
when: Every figure, so every beat moves with the same physics.
why: Measured on a real cut and held up in review.

name: One graphic per 15 to 25 s, no bullet lists
what: A talking head gets about one graphic every 15 to 25 seconds; never a bullet list on screen, never a graphic that only restates the sentence.
when: Always on a talking head. A stretch with no graphic is allowed; say it is deliberate.
why: A first cut with eight beats lost three in review; a list on screen is a slide.

name: Every number on screen is real
what: A number shown is the user's real figure with its source, or the beat does not ship; never a placeholder.
when: Always.
why: A placeholder number is not a placeholder to the viewer; a reference cut lost a beat because of one.

name: The real product, never a drawing of it
what: When the speaker names their product, show a real screenshot or recording, cropped to what carries the point, never a drawn impression or a drawn device frame.
when: Always. Offer to blur real people's names and e-mails on screen.
why: A bare screen reads as a recording; a drawn laptop reads as clip art.

name: Your brand, set once
what: The user's name, colours, logo, fonts and notes from workspace/brand/ fill every style's brand slots, without overriding what makes the style.
when: Every run when the brand is set: do not ask for what it holds; never write into workspace/brand/ during an edit.
why: Making the skills the user's own is a major goal of the app.

name: Logos as one set
what: Several logos shown together share one square size, one corner radius and one optical inset; only things the speaker names get a vendor's logo.
when: Whenever several logos appear together.
why: Three marks with three different corners read as three screenshots, not as a set.

name: Green and red keep their meaning
what: Green means it worked and red means it did not, whatever the brand palette says; brand hex values come from the brand guide, never eyeballed.
when: Always.
why: Written as a rule of the brand kit.

name: Captions in the speaker's own words
what: Captions and on-screen words come from words.json, in the language spoken, never translated or paraphrased; always pass --lang to the transcription.
when: Always.
why: Auto-detection once translated a whole take with confidence 1.00 and shipped for several rounds.

name: The picture settles the names
what: Product names, acronyms and jargon the transcript mangles are checked on a frame of the speaker's screen or with the user, then fixed as word patterns, never indices.
when: Every edit, before captions.
why: The transcript locates, it never attests; index-based fixes rot when the transcript shifts.

name: Words on screen on a vertical short
what: A vertical short always carries the words on screen, because most feeds autoplay muted.
when: Every vertical short.
why: Most feeds autoplay muted, so the words carry the opening.

name: The feed's safe zones
what: Text, important elements and the face stay inside x 0.095 to 0.905, y 0.128 to 0.774; never in the bottom band (y 0.79 and below) or the button column (x 0.84 and right, from y 0.425 down).
when: Every vertical video, every style. Check with the overlay tool on the video or a still.
why: Ihsane brought two Reel screenshots with the zones in red: « je crois que nous, on a fait cette erreur-là »; headlines sat over the tabs.

name: Words below the head on a tight shot
what: When the head fills the top of the safe area, the words go below the head, in front of the speaker, the block's bottom on y 0.765.
when: A tight shot where the head starts around y 0.13 to 0.15. Never squeezed against the top edge.
why: Part of the safe-zone rules set that day.

name: Text behind the speaker is measured
what: Every word on the under layer is measured 15 times a second, through the same camera, for the share the speaker's mask hides: 18 % means look at it, 30 % is rejected.
when: Every headline that passes behind the speaker. Removing a word that carries nothing beats hiding it.
why: On the first pass words were 40 % to 100 % hidden, invisible on random previews; an L behind the hair reads as an I.

name: No script font white on white
what: A script word crossing an Impact word goes across a yellow word, or gets its own line; never white script over white Impact.
when: Always with a script accent.
why: White script across a white Impact word disappears; across yellow it reads, as in the reviewer's reference.

name: Matte holes for what the speaker holds
what: A rectangle cut out of the person mask where the body is not, so a held laptop does not show through a window coming out from behind the speaker.
when: When the speaker holds an object and a graphic must pass in front of it; place the edge from edges.json, keep the masks grey.
why: Vision counts what a person holds as part of them; a threshold does not fix it.
doc: references/pitfalls.md § What the speaker holds is not the speaker: matteHoles

name: The Pipecorn generic
what: About six seconds at the very end: the sparkle bursts into Pipecorn yellow, the wordmark, then values rolling in one slot with their number in a black pill, then Pipecorn again, with effects only and no music.
when: A bonus of every style, asked every time with the first question, never on by default; run last, on the delivered file.
why: Ihsane validated it after three refused versions; a reminder of Pipecorn's value that changes from video to video.
doc: references/pipecorn-generic.md § What it is (validated: do not re-open)

name: Generic on a dark stage
what: A version of the Pipecorn generic played on a dark stage.
when: Never.
why: Too far from the style it ended.
doc: references/pipecorn-generic.md § The Pipecorn generic: a bonus of every style

name: Generic as one static page
what: A version of the generic with everything laid out on one page at once.
when: Never.
why: It was not dynamic.
doc: references/pipecorn-generic.md § The Pipecorn generic: a bonus of every style

name: Numbers before their words
what: A generic that shows a number first, alone, or counting up, before the words that say what it measures.
when: Never. The words come first, the number 0.5 s later in the pill; never a number alone, never a count-up.
why: A version with numbers first did not say what they measured.
doc: references/pipecorn-generic.md § What it is (validated: do not re-open)

name: Synthesised sound effects
what: Effects generated in code from noise sweeps and sines (taps, a shutter, a metallic hit, pops) instead of real recordings.
when: Never for a delivered video's effects: only real recordings from the packs on the shelf.
why: The synthesised set was refused; the SFX pack's files replaced them. The small sounds felt dated, « like 2012 ».
doc: references/audio-spec.md § The SFX pack on the vertical short (2026-09-29, v5)

name: The Top 5 SFX pack, one role each
what: Five real recordings, one role each: the click for what appears, the camera flash for a change of shot, the whoosh for a transition, the glitch for one text pop, the riser into a payoff (its dead stop is the accent).
when: The big moves of every vertical short, 9 to 11 LU under the programme, each placed by its measured attack (align).
why: The reviewer sent the pack and, after hearing the result, asked for the skill to use it by default.
doc: references/audio-spec.md § The SFX pack on the vertical short (2026-09-29, v5)

name: Light sounds of what appears (Motionix)
what: Every element that appears gets a very light sound of its own from the Motionix pack (a pop, a swish, a tick, a confirm, a deny), 15 to 20 LU under the programme, each role rotating its files.
when: Small appearances; the big moves keep the Top 5. A light sound within 0.15 s of a big one, or 70 ms of another light one, is dropped.
why: The reviewer sent the pack to add many more very light little sounds and asked for it in the references.
doc: references/audio-spec.md § The light sounds of what appears: the Motionix pack

name: A pen sound on every stroke
what: A pencil or marker sound under every drawn stroke or written word, or the same pen sound repeated.
when: Never. A pen is allowed only when the drawing IS the beat, at the bottom of the mix; never as the sound of text arriving.
why: The same pencil every time was extremely repetitive; a sound on every pencil stroke was found horrible, far too many.
doc: references/audio-spec.md § The theatrical pass: no pen at all (2026-09-07)

name: One cue per event, spaced
what: One sound per event, not per element; no two effects inside 250 ms; about 0.6 cues per second at most; one gesture of a repeated figure is heard, not all.
when: Every mix. A stop-motion ratchet and samples under a tear are exempt.
why: The reviewer asked for far fewer animation sounds; a tick on every row was a few too many.
doc: references/audio-spec.md § What the chosen intro actually keeps

name: A synthesised music bed
what: A bed composed in code note by note (a lo-fi loop of sines, a supersaw EDM bed).
when: Never by default: a cut ships without a bed until the user has chosen one from a listening board with real tracks.
why: Two synth beds were rejected in review: the lo-fi loop called ridiculous, the supersaw bed still disliked.
doc: references/audio-spec.md § A music bed: synthesised here, and say so

name: The music shelf
what: Tracks that passed a listening session, with their measured loudness and cue gain, prepared on a beat with a low-pass sweep and fade into the cut.
when: Offer the shelf first on every new video; Hip Hop 02 was chosen on 2026-09-04.
why: The search and the listening session are already paid for.
doc: references/audio-spec.md § A music bed: synthesised here, and say so

name: Say it when a track can be claimed
what: Tracks not from Mixkit may be claimed by Content ID and block monetisation: allowed, but say it once to the user, in one line, before the render.
when: Whenever one of those tracks is picked.
why: Ihsane: allowed in a video, but they can block its monetisation.

name: Landscape bed at −46 dB
what: In the landscape intro, the bed sits at about −46 dB mean on the effects bus under a −14 LUFS programme, far lower than on a short.
when: The landscape intro only; never carried over to a short.
why: Bracketed by review: at −55 it could not be heard, −41 was a little too loud, −46 was validated.
doc: references/audio-spec.md § A music bed: synthesised here, and say so

name: The landscape bed level on a short
what: A short's bed set at the landscape intro's level (about 33 LU, or 25 LU, under the voice).
when: Never on a short.
why: Both versions were sent back: even the louder one was not loud enough.
doc: references/audio-spec.md § A music bed: synthesised here, and say so

name: Bed 15 LU under the voice on a short
what: On a short, the bed aims 12 to 15 LU under the voice as heard, measured by subtraction, never by arithmetic.
when: Every short; measure on every edit, a level does not carry over.
why: Retested at 15 LU on the vertical short; the reviewer's verdict is pending.
doc: references/audio-spec.md § A music bed: synthesised here, and say so

name: Your voice made better (voice isolator)
what: ElevenLabs' voice isolator removes the room's echo and the noise, at the take's exact length, picture copied untouched.
when: A bonus of every skill where the user's real voice is heard, asked every time, never on by default; run before anything reads the sound. Needs the ElevenLabs key; never block a run on it.
why: Ihsane heard five versions of his take side by side: the plain isolated voice won.

name: Home-made voice clean-up
what: A light ffmpeg clean-up, a home-made anti-echo, or the isolator with a studio treatment on top.
when: Not as the voice bonus: the plain isolator replaced them. The room EQ (voiceChain) stays a measured fallback, about 1.1 dB of gain movement inside speech at most.
why: All three lost to the plain isolated voice in Ihsane's side-by-side listening.

name: −14 LUFS, −1 dBTP
what: Every master targets −14 LUFS integrated and −1.0 dBTP true peak with two-pass loudnorm, aiming 0.6 dB under the ceiling for the AAC encode; never a bare volume boost.
when: Every delivered video.
why: A standard, not a taste: platforms normalise and mostly only turn content down.
doc: references/audio-spec.md § Loudness: a standard, not a taste

name: An HDR take stays HDR
what: A phone take in HLG HDR keeps its pixels, bit depth, codec family and colour tags; it is never converted to SDR unasked.
when: Always; a tone map only when asked (--tonemap).
why: An HDR to SDR conversion is a grading decision on someone else's footage; it was rejected immediately the one time it shipped unasked.

name: Converting HDR to SDR unasked
what: Tone-mapping a phone's HDR take to SDR as part of an edit, without being asked.
when: Never unasked.
why: It moves contrast, saturation and skin tone; it was rejected immediately the one time it shipped.

name: Cut only in measured silence
what: A rush is cut on breath groups, where the envelope says the voice really stops (within 10 dB of the floor for 140 ms), plus 200 ms of breath; where speech runs on, a 110 ms fade at the local minimum.
when: Every rush or derush. Never on the transcript's word times or a fixed padding.
why: Fixed padding clipped 23 of 40 segments; clipped word ends are the defect users hear first.

name: Check a join by transcribing it again
what: A cut boundary is verified by re-transcribing the window around it, never by measuring the level at the cut; then the rendered file is transcribed as the ground truth.
when: Every join of a rush.
why: A clipped word changes what the model hears: « you cannot » becomes « you can ».

name: Measure, do not assert
what: Every statement about a cut (sync, levels, coverage, loudness) comes from a number the verify script produces, and the numbers are told to the user.
when: Before every delivery.
why: Claude cannot watch or listen; a measurement that contradicts expectation is usually right.

name: Audition sounds by role
what: Every candidate sound rendered to a WAV at the same peak so a human can pick, offered per role with the current design first.
when: When the user wants to hear sound options.
why: Status not written in the docs; the reviewer asked to hear several options and Claude cannot listen.

name: Talk like to a friend
what: A script sounds like the user talking to a friend in front of them: tell, do not present; I and you, contractions, short sentences (12 words, 16 at most), their own expressions.
when: Every script the video skills write.
why: Ihsane: « comme si je parlais à un pote en face de moi, simple… »
doc: references/how-you-talk.md § Like talking to a friend sitting in front of you

name: Simple English, checked
what: Words a B1 speaker uses every day: no idioms, no marketing words, no French built into English, no hard long words; a word list is checked by the scripts and refused with its simple replacement.
when: Every script; the list is a floor, read the script aloud as the user.
why: Ihsane is not a native English speaker: « il faut utiliser des mots simples ».
doc: references/how-you-talk.md § Simple English (the user is not a native speaker)

name: Voice-over timed on what was heard
what: ElevenLabs reads the whole text in one take, then every word gets its time from what Scribe hears on that take, never from the synthesis's own alignment.
when: Every voice-over of the motion and voice-over skills.
why: The synthesis's alignment is 50 to 250 ms off, which shows on one-word captions.

name: Say one passage again
what: One passage of a voice-over said again, the rest of the take untouched.
when: When one passage of a voice-over is wrong.
why: Status not written in the docs.

name: Sticker of a named thing
what: A cut-out of a thing the voice names (a product, a tool, an object), with a white outline and a soft shadow, made with Nano Banana 2 on flat green or from a picture the user has.
when: The moment the voice names the thing; look at the sources before picking one.
why: Status not written in the docs.

name: A real public page, captured
what: A public web page (an official page, a pricing page, a product's screen) captured sharp with no browser bar, or one section of it.
when: To show the real thing. Never a page behind a login, never a form filled in.
why: Written as a rule of the tool: never behind a login.

name: A picture made with Nano Banana 2
what: A picture made for the video (a sticker source, a reportage-style photo of what no shot shows, a document's background), billed to the user's key, re-encoded as JPEG.
when: When no real shot or picture exists.
why: Status not written in the docs.

name: B-roll shots from YouTube
what: Shots searched on YouTube, looked at on contact sheets, then only the seconds kept are cut into a shared library per subject, with their source and licence.
when: When the video needs real shots of a subject; never with a browser's cookies, spaced requests.
why: Status not written in the docs.

name: Annotate a real document
what: A real document or PDF page drawn on white, its text found with its boxes, so a word is marked where it is the moment the voice says it.
when: When the video shows an official form, a report or a notice.
why: Status not written in the docs.

name: Open-licence default faces
what: When the brand has no fonts, the motion skills draw with SIL Open Font License faces fetched once (Archivo, Onest, Bricolage Grotesque, Fraunces, Instrument Serif, Caveat); the brand's own fonts come first.
when: Every motion run without brand fonts.
why: Written as the rule of the kit: the brand's own fonts come first.

name: Frames drawn in HTML by headless Chrome
what: The films are HTML pages drawn as a pure function of time, rendered frame by frame by a headless Chrome.
when: The motion and voice-over skills' renders.
why: Status not written in the docs.
